opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a question I think about a lot, and I'd say my answer is "it depends." Synthetic data can be really valuable, but it comes with risks you have to take seriously.

On the value side, the most obvious benefit is control. With real-world data you get whatever the world happens to have photographed, with all the biases and gaps that come with that. With generated images you can fill those gaps on purpose. You can make rare cases, odd viewpoints, unusual lighting, or combinations of objects that almost never show up together in natural photos. You also get labels almost for free. If you know what you asked the generator for, you often know the ground truth, whether that's segmentation, depth, or the attributes of the scene. For a lot of vision tasks, getting accurate dense labels on real images is very expensive, so that matters a lot.

There's also a practical side around privacy and licensing. If you can produce useful training data without scraping people's faces or copyrighted work, that's attractive. I'd add a caveat, though. The generator was trained on something, so you haven't really escaped those questions, you've just moved them one step back.

On the risk side, the thing I worry about most is a kind of feedback loop. Generative models don't sample the full distribution of real images evenly. They tend to favor the high-probability, "typical" regions and under-represent the tails. If you train on their output, and especially if the next generation of generators is trained on that, you can get a gradual narrowing, where diversity drops and the strange but real parts of the visual world disappear. People sometimes call this model collapse. Even short of collapse, you can quietly bake in the generator's particular look: its textures, its lighting priors, the subtle artifacts it always leaves. A downstream model can learn shortcuts based on those artifacts and then do worse on real photos.

There's also a quieter issue with evaluation. If synthetic images end up in your test sets, or if the web fills up with generated content you can't reliably detect, you start losing track of what "real-world performance" means. That's partly why I think provenance and detection work matters. It isn't only about misinformation. It's also about knowing what's actually in our datasets.

So in practice my view is that synthetic data works best as a supplement and not a replacement. Ground it in real data, use generation for targeted things like rare cases, augmentation, and dense labels, and always measure on held-out real data. If you treat it as a tool for filling specific gaps, it can be very powerful. If you treat it as a free, infinite substitute for the real world, I think that's where you get into trouble.

r001.rationale: The response says training on generated outputs can pass along the generator’s textures, lighting priors, and artifacts, which downstream models can learn as shortcuts.

r002.rationale: It describes synthetic data as useful, but does not state that synthetic images need to be distilled or filtered to sufficiently high quality to benefit training.

r003.rationale: It discusses provenance and detecting generated content, but does not pose the question of which generated data is worth training on and which should be excluded.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, it's a question I get asked a lot, and I think the honest answer is that it's genuinely a double-edged thing. On the value side, synthetic data is incredibly attractive because you get control. When you're collecting real images, you're stuck with whatever distribution the world happens to give you, and that distribution has all sorts of gaps and biases baked in. With generated images, you can say, I want more examples of this rare category, or this lighting condition, or this pose that almost never shows up in natural photos, and you can just make them. You can also get perfect labels for free in a lot of cases, because you know exactly what you asked the model to produce, or if you're rendering through a pipeline, you know the depth, the segmentation, the geometry. That's really hard to get at scale with real data.

The risk side is where I think people need to be more careful than they often are. The first problem is that a generative model only knows what it's seen. So if you train on its outputs, you're not adding new information about the world, you're resampling from an approximation of it, and that approximation has its own artifacts and blind spots. There's been a bunch of work on this collapse effect, where if you iterate the loop, models trained on generated data, which then generate data for the next model, the distribution narrows and the tails disappear. You lose exactly the diversity you were hoping to gain.

The second problem is subtler. Generated images tend to look plausible to a human, but they have statistical signatures that a model will pick up on. Textures that are a little too smooth, certain frequency characteristics, a particular way of rendering hands or text or reflections. A downstream model can learn those as features, and then it performs well on synthetic data and worse on real data, and you may not notice until you deploy.

So the way I think about it in practice is that synthetic data is best used as a supplement, not a replacement. It's great for filling specific holes, for augmentation, for bootstrapping when real data is expensive or impossible to collect, like some safety-critical or privacy-sensitive scenarios. But I'd always want real data anchoring the distribution, and I'd want to be evaluating on real data, held out, so that the synthetic stuff can't fool you about how well you're actually doing. And it's worth being deliberate about provenance. If you don't track what's generated and what isn't, you'll eventually end up training on your own outputs without realizing it, and that's where a lot of the degradation comes from.

r001.rationale: The response says downstream models may learn synthetic artifacts as features, but it does not clearly state that poor-quality generated images cause a model to reproduce those defects.

r002.rationale: It describes synthetic data as useful for augmentation and filling gaps, but does not say that synthetic images distilled to sufficiently high quality benefit training.

r003.rationale: It recommends tracking generated versus real data, but does not raise the problem of deciding which generated images are suitable for training and which should be excluded.

astra-6.text:
I think there’s a lot of potential there, particularly because you can control what you generate. If you’re missing certain kinds of examples in your dataset, you can try to create those examples, and you can generate variations that would be expensive to collect in the real world.

But the question is whether you’re actually adding useful information. A generated image reflects what the generator has learned, including its biases and its limitations. So generating a million images doesn’t necessarily give you a million independent examples of the world. You might just be reproducing the same blind spots at a larger scale.

There’s also a distinction between an image that looks convincing to us and an image that provides the right training signal. For example, if you’re trying to learn geometry, a realistic-looking image can still have inconsistent geometry. A downstream model might learn those inconsistencies, or pick up on artifacts that don’t exist in real photographs.

So I’d think of synthetic data as a tool for augmenting real data, with validation on real examples that are independent of the generation process. The interesting question is less, ‘Can we make more images?’ and more, ‘Which images actually help the model learn something it couldn’t learn before?’

r001.rationale: It says a downstream model might learn inconsistencies or artifacts in generated images, and that generated data can reproduce the generator’s blind spots.

r002.rationale: The response says synthetic images might help and should be validated, but does not state that sufficiently high quality synthetic images can benefit training.

r003.rationale: It asks which generated images actually help the model learn and contrasts useful training signal with images that merely reproduce limitations or artifacts.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the value is that you get a lot more control over your training data. You can generate examples of situations that are rare or difficult to capture, and you can vary things like the background, lighting, or viewpoint. That’s useful both for filling gaps in a dataset and for testing what a model is actually learning.

The risk is that generating more images doesn’t necessarily give you more information. A generator has its own biases and limitations, and those can get passed on to the model you’re training. You can also introduce artifacts that make the training task artificially easy. The model learns something that works on synthetic images but doesn’t transfer to real ones.

So I’d think of synthetic data as a tool for addressing specific gaps, with the value measured on real, held-out data. The question isn’t just, ‘Do these images look convincing?’ It’s, ‘Do they help the model perform better in the situations we care about?’

r001.rationale: It says generator biases and artifacts can affect training, but does not state that poor-quality generated images cause the model to reproduce their defects.

r002.rationale: It describes synthetic data as useful for filling gaps, but does not say that sufficiently high-quality synthetic images benefit training.

r003.rationale: It asks whether synthetic images improve performance, but does not pose the problem of separating generated data worth training on from data to exclude.
